events.fact: President Benjamin Harrison signed the act of Congress establishing Yosemite National Park in California, setting aside over 1,500 square miles of wilderness as a public trust.
The Ford Motor Company shipped its first Model T to a customer, the fruit of Henry Ford's long labor to build a sturdy automobile the common man could afford.

block: On October 1, 1890, President Benjamin Harrison signed the act of Congress that set aside Yosemite as a national park, guarding more than a thousand square miles of valley, sequoia, and granite as a common trust for the generations to come. On the same day in 1908, Henry Ford shipped the first Model T to its owner, the reward of dogged years at the workbench that would soon put a dependable machine within reach of the ordinary working family. A Steadfast citizen keeps at the long labor entrusted to him as Ford kept at his, and he guards what God has given into his hand rather than squandering it, knowing that faithful stewardship outlasts a single lifetime.

events.fact: Major John André, the British officer who conspired with the traitor Benedict Arnold to surrender West Point, was hanged as a spy at Tappan, New York, by order of General George Washington.
Charles Schulz's comic strip 'Peanuts' first appeared in seven American newspapers, beginning a humble daily labor that would run for half a century.

block: On October 2, 1780, Major John André was hanged as a spy at Tappan, New York, condemned by a board of officers for his part in Benedict Arnold's plot to betray West Point, a sober reminder that treachery against one's country ends in shame while fidelity endures. On the same day in 1950, Charles Schulz's 'Peanuts' debuted in seven newspapers, the quiet beginning of a daily strip he would draw faithfully for fifty years without missing his appointed work. A Steadfast citizen learns from both that a man's worth is proven by constancy, keeping faith where André broke it and pressing on at his daily task as Schulz did, day after unbroken day, before the God who sees every hidden labor.

events.fact: President George Washington issued the first national Thanksgiving Proclamation under the Constitution, appointing Thursday, November 26, as a day of public thanksgiving and prayer to God.
President Abraham Lincoln issued his Thanksgiving Proclamation, setting apart the last Thursday of November as a national day of thanks to 'our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the heavens.'

block: On October 3, 1789, President George Washington issued the first national Thanksgiving Proclamation under the new Constitution, calling the people of the United States to set apart a day to render unto Almighty God their sincere and humble thanks for His many favors. On the same day in 1863, in the dark middle of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln took up Washington's example and proclaimed the last Thursday of November a day of thanksgiving and praise to our beneficent Father in heaven. A Steadfast citizen keeps a thankful heart in both plenty and peril, bowing as these presidents did before the God whose mercies do not fail though the times grow hard.

events.fact: American forces under General William Henry Harrison won the Battle of the Thames in Upper Canada, a decisive victory in the War of 1812 that secured the Northwest for the United States.
President Harry Truman delivered the first presidential address televised from the White House, asking Americans to conserve grain to feed a starving, war-ravaged Europe.

block: On October 5, 1813, General William Henry Harrison and his men won the Battle of the Thames, breaking the British and allied force in Upper Canada and securing the Northwest frontier for the young United States in the War of 1812. On the same day in 1947, President Harry Truman gave the first televised address from the White House, asking his countrymen to go without grain and meat on set days so that famine-stricken Europe might be fed. A Steadfast citizen holds his post whether on the battle line or at his own table, standing firm in the field as Harrison did and denying himself for his neighbor's sake, trusting God to honor a people who endure hardship for what is right.

events.fact: Thirteen German Mennonite and Quaker families from Krefeld, led by Francis Daniel Pastorius, landed near Philadelphia and founded Germantown, the first German settlement in America, seeking freedom of conscience.
The Reno brothers carried out the first train robbery in American history near Seymour, Indiana, seizing some thirteen thousand dollars from an Ohio and Mississippi Railroad car.

block: On October 6, 1683, thirteen German families led by Francis Daniel Pastorius landed near Philadelphia and laid out Germantown, crossing an ocean to worship God freely and build an honest community in the Pennsylvania wilderness. On the same day in 1866, the Reno brothers staged the first train robbery in the nation's history near Seymour, Indiana, a lawless act that opened a long and bloody chapter on the frontier and reminds us how quickly liberty curdles into license when men cast off the fear of God. A Steadfast citizen plants himself with the Germantown settlers, laboring patiently within the law for his family and his church rather than grasping at his neighbor's goods, for the man who endures in honest work is built upon the Rock.

events.fact: The Stamp Act Congress convened in New York City, where delegates from nine colonies met to draw up a lawful, united declaration of their grievances against Parliament's taxes.

Patriot militia, the Overmountain Men, defeated and killed Loyalist commander Major Patrick Ferguson at the Battle of Kings Mountain in South Carolina, turning the tide of the war's southern campaign.

block: On October 7, 1765, the Stamp Act Congress gathered in New York City, where delegates from nine colonies set their hands to a reasoned and united protest, choosing lawful petition over riot to defend the liberties of free men. On the same day in 1780, the rough frontier riflemen known as the Overmountain Men climbed Kings Mountain in South Carolina and crushed the Loyalist force under Major Patrick Ferguson, a stunning victory that revived the Patriot cause after a string of defeats. A Steadfast citizen stands his ground as those backwoodsmen stood theirs, and like the men of the Stamp Act Congress he holds firm to ordered liberty, trusting God to strengthen those who will not bend to tyranny.

events.fact: The Great Chicago Fire broke out on the night of October 8, burning for three days, destroying some 17,000 structures, and leaving over 100,000 residents homeless.

Corporal Alvin C. York, a devout Tennessee Christian, led a small detachment in the Argonne Forest of France, silencing German machine guns, killing some twenty-five and capturing 132 prisoners; he was awarded the Medal of Honor.

block: On October 8, 1871, fire broke out in Chicago and raged for three days, leaving a great city in ashes and more than a hundred thousand people homeless, a humbling visitation that drove a proud people to rebuild in chastened hope. On the same day in 1918, Corporal Alvin York, a backwoods believer who had wrestled hard with the lawfulness of war before submitting to his duty, led a handful of men against the German guns in the Argonne and brought back 132 prisoners. An Obedient citizen submits himself as York did, bowing first to conscience and then to the lawful call of his country, and he humbles himself under the mighty hand of God who both chastens cities and strengthens the willing soldier.

events.fact: Roger Williams was banished from the Massachusetts Bay Colony for his insistence on liberty of conscience; he would found Providence as a refuge open to all seeking freedom to worship.
The General Court of Connecticut passed an act to erect a Collegiate School, the institution that became Yale, founded to train young men for the ministry and public service.

block: On October 9, 1635, the General Court of Massachusetts banished Roger Williams for refusing to bend his conscience, and rather than recant he carried his convictions into the wilderness and founded Providence as a haven for all who sought to worship God freely. On the same day in 1701, the Connecticut court passed its act to erect the Collegiate School that would become Yale, raised up to train faithful men for the pulpit and the magistracy. A Trustworthy citizen keeps faith with his conscience as Williams did and helps build institutions worthy to be trusted with the next generation, proving himself dependable before God in matters both small and great.

events.fact: The United States Naval Academy was founded at Fort Severn in Annapolis, Maryland, by Secretary of the Navy George Bancroft, opening with fifty midshipmen and seven professors.
Inventor John Wesley Hyatt received a U.S. patent for an improved billiard ball, part of the patient experimentation that would lead him to invent celluloid, an early manufactured plastic.

block: On October 10, 1845, Secretary of the Navy George Bancroft quietly founded the Naval School at Annapolis with fifty midshipmen and seven instructors, building an honorable academy to form young officers in duty and seamanship. On the same day in 1865, John Wesley Hyatt earned a patent for a better billiard ball, one fruit of the persistent tinkering that soon yielded celluloid and a new American industry. A Trustworthy citizen proves himself in steady preparation as the midshipmen of Annapolis did, and labors honestly at his craft as Hyatt did at his bench, becoming the kind of man on whom others may safely rely under God.

events.fact: The small American fleet under Benedict Arnold fought the British on Lake Champlain at the Battle of Valcour Island; though most ships were lost, the stand delayed the British advance and helped set the stage for the victory at Saratoga.

Apollo 7, the first crewed flight of the Apollo program, launched from Cape Kennedy with astronauts Wally Schirra, Donn Eisele, and Walter Cunningham, restoring the manned program after the Apollo 1 fire.

block: On October 11, 1776, a hastily built American fleet made its stand against a stronger British force at Valcour Island on Lake Champlain, and though the little squadron was shattered, its stubborn fight cost the enemy precious weeks and helped secure the war-winning victory at Saratoga the next year. On the same day in 1968, Apollo 7 carried Wally Schirra and his crew into orbit, the first manned flight to fly after three astronauts had perished in the Apollo 1 fire, proving the nation would press on through grief toward the moon. A Steadfast citizen refuses to quit when the cost is high, holding the line as those sailors did and rising again after disaster as those astronauts did, certain that God honors those who endure to the end.

events.fact: The Continental Congress in Philadelphia authorized the first armed vessels of a national fleet, the act now honored as the birthday of the United States Navy.
The cornerstone of the President's House, later known as the White House, was laid in the new federal city of Washington under the direction of architect James Hoban.

block: On October 13, 1775, the Continental Congress voted to fit out armed vessels to defend American shores, laying the keel of what would become the United States Navy in the very season the colonies took up arms. On the same day in 1792, workmen laid the cornerstone of the President's House in the raw new capital, beginning the executive mansion that every president since John Adams has called home. An Upright citizen helps lay sound foundations as those founders did, whether the timbers of a navy or the stone of a great house, building straight and true in the fear of God so that what he raises will stand for those who come after.

events.fact: Former President Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest by a would-be assassin in Milwaukee, yet, with the bullet lodged in him, delivered his full campaign speech before seeking treatment.
Test pilot Captain Chuck Yeager became the first man to fly faster than sound, breaking the sound barrier in the Bell X-1 over the Mojave Desert in California.

block: On October 14, 1912, Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest while campaigning in Milwaukee, and with the assassin's bullet still in his body he steadied himself and spoke for an hour and a half, declaring it took more than a bullet to stop him. On the same day in 1947, Captain Chuck Yeager pushed the rocket-powered Bell X-1 past the speed of sound over the Mojave, breaking a barrier many had feared no man could survive. A Steadfast citizen presses through pain and fear to finish his appointed work, bearing up under the blow as Roosevelt did and pressing past the unknown as Yeager did, asking God for the iron will to see the task through.

events.fact: Eleven-year-old Grace Bedell wrote to candidate Abraham Lincoln urging him to grow a beard; Lincoln later did so and, on his way to his inauguration, stopped his train to seek the girl out by name.
The Edison Electric Light Company began operation, the enterprise Thomas Edison founded to carry forward his long and costly labor to perfect a practical electric light.

block: On October 15, 1860, a girl named Grace Bedell wrote to Abraham Lincoln advising him to grow whiskers, and the busy candidate not only answered her kindly but, months later as president-elect, halted his train at Westfield to find her in the crowd and keep faith with a child. On the same day in 1878, Thomas Edison launched the Edison Electric Light Company, staking it on the stubborn years of toil and a thousand failed experiments that would finally bring light into the homes of ordinary men. A Steadfast citizen keeps the small promise as faithfully as the great one, honoring his word as Lincoln did and refusing to abandon the long task as Edison did, knowing God marks the man who is constant in little things.

events.fact: At Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, dentist William Morton gave ether to a patient while surgeon John Collins Warren painlessly removed a tumor, the first public demonstration of surgical anesthesia.
Abraham Lincoln delivered his Peoria Speech in Illinois, a powerful moral and constitutional argument against the spread of slavery that revived his political career.

block: On October 16, 1846, in the surgical theater of Massachusetts General Hospital, William Morton administered ether while Dr. John Collins Warren cut without pain, an hour that conquered the agony of surgery and opened the way to countless lives mercifully spared. On the same day in 1854, Abraham Lincoln rose at Peoria and laid out a careful, conscience-stirring case against extending slavery into the territories, fixing his feet on moral ground he would never abandon. A Steadfast citizen labors to ease his neighbor's suffering as those physicians did and stands immovable on what is right as Lincoln did, holding fast to truth and mercy alike under the eye of God.

events.fact: British General John Burgoyne surrendered his army of over 6,000 men to American General Horatio Gates at Saratoga, New York, the turning point that brought France into the war as America's ally.

The Loma Prieta earthquake, magnitude 6.9, struck the San Francisco Bay area minutes before a World Series game, killing 63; the timing kept the freeways unusually empty and spared far greater loss of life.

block: On October 17, 1777, General John Burgoyne laid down the arms of his whole army to General Horatio Gates at Saratoga, a victory so complete that it persuaded France to ally with the struggling colonies and proved the great turning point of the Revolution. On the same day in 1989, a violent earthquake shook the San Francisco Bay just before a World Series game, and though it killed sixty-three, the very hour it struck had emptied the crowded freeways and mercifully held back a far greater toll. A Steadfast citizen stands firm in the day of trial, persevering as the Continentals did at Saratoga and rebuilding after the ground itself is shaken, trusting the sovereign God who governs both the fortunes of war and the trembling of the earth.

events.fact: The United States formally took possession of Alaska from Russia in a flag ceremony at Sitka, completing the purchase arranged by Secretary of State William Seward for $7.2 million.
American forces raised the United States flag over Puerto Rico, formalizing the transfer of the island under the terms ending the Spanish-American War.

block: On October 18, 1867, soldiers paraded at Sitka as the Russian flag came down and the Stars and Stripes rose over Alaska, completing under treaty the vast purchase that William Seward's foresight had secured for the nation. On the same day in 1898, American troops raised the flag over Puerto Rico as Spanish rule gave way at the close of the war, sovereignty passing in ordered and lawful fashion. An Obedient citizen honors the rule of law by which nations are bound and lands are duly transferred, submitting himself to rightful authority as the Scriptures command and trusting God, who sets the bounds of peoples' habitation.

events.fact: British General Lord Cornwallis surrendered his army of some 8,000 men to General George Washington and the allied French forces at Yorktown, Virginia, effectively ending the Revolutionary War.

At the Battle of Cedar Creek in Virginia, General Philip Sheridan rallied his retreating Union army after a furious ride from Winchester and turned a near-defeat into a decisive victory in the Shenandoah Valley.

block: On October 19, 1781, Lord Cornwallis surrendered his trapped army to General Washington and his French allies at Yorktown, the blow that broke Britain's will to fight and won American independence after long years of sacrifice. On the same day in 1864, General Philip Sheridan, hearing the guns from Winchester, galloped twelve miles to the field at Cedar Creek and rallied his broken men, turning a morning's rout into an evening's triumph. A Responsible citizen sees his duty through to the end as Washington did, and refuses to surrender to a bad beginning as Sheridan refused, shouldering the burden God lays on him until the work is finished.

events.fact: The United States Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase Treaty, acquiring the western half of the Mississippi basin from France and doubling the size of the nation.

American and British diplomats signed the Convention of 1818, fixing the 49th parallel as the boundary between the United States and British North America and opening the frontier to peaceful settlement.

block: On October 20, 1803, the Senate ratified the treaty for the Louisiana Purchase, and at roughly four cents an acre the young Republic doubled its size and opened a continent of frontier to its people. On the same day in 1818, American and British negotiators set the boundary along the 49th parallel, drawing in peace a line that spared two nations from war and made the long western settlement possible. A Steadfast citizen takes the long view as those statesmen did, laboring patiently to extend and secure what is good for the generations not yet born, and trusting God to prosper the work of faithful and far-sighted hands.

events.fact: The frigate USS Constitution was launched in Boston Harbor with President John Adams present; she earned the name 'Old Ironsides' in the War of 1812 and remains the oldest commissioned warship afloat.
Thomas Edison and his team at Menlo Park, New Jersey, tested an incandescent lamp that burned for over thirteen hours, the breakthrough that made practical electric light a reality.

block: On October 21, 1797, the great frigate USS Constitution slid into Boston Harbor as President John Adams looked on, a stout-hearted ship whose oak sides would turn British cannon in the War of 1812 and earn her the immortal name Old Ironsides. On the same day in 1879, after more than a thousand patient experiments, Thomas Edison watched a carbon-filament lamp glow steadily for over thirteen hours at Menlo Park, lighting the path to the electric age. A Steadfast citizen is built to endure as that frigate was built, and he keeps faith with a long labor as Edison kept faith with his, refusing to quit until the thing is proven and giving God the glory for strength to persevere.

events.fact: Union forces won the Battle of Westport near Kansas City, the largest battle west of the Mississippi River and the engagement that broke Confederate power in Missouri.
A suicide truck bomb destroyed the U.S. Marine barracks in Beirut, Lebanon, killing 241 American servicemen, mostly Marines, the Corps' greatest single-day loss since Iwo Jima.

block: On October 23, 1864, Union troops prevailed at the Battle of Westport near Kansas City, the largest clash fought west of the Mississippi, ending the Confederate threat to Missouri and the western frontier. On the same day in 1983, a truck laden with explosives tore through the Marine barracks in Beirut and killed 241 American servicemen as they slept, the bloodiest single day the Corps had known since Iwo Jima. A Steadfast citizen honors such men by holding fast to duty and faith even unto death, grieving the fallen yet not without hope, for the God who keeps watch over the souls of His servants will wipe away every tear and raise up those who were faithful.

events.fact: The Western Union Telegraph Company completed the first transcontinental telegraph line at Salt Lake City, allowing instant communication between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts for the first time.
The George Washington Bridge over the Hudson River was dedicated, opening eight months ahead of schedule as the longest suspension bridge in the world at that time.

block: On October 24, 1861, crews of the Western Union company joined the eastern and western wires at Salt Lake City, completing the transcontinental telegraph and letting a message leap from coast to coast in moments where it once took weeks. On the same day in 1931, the great George Washington Bridge was dedicated across the Hudson, finished ahead of schedule and longer than any suspension span yet built by the hand of man. A Steadfast citizen joins himself to great and patient works as these builders did, knowing the line that spans a continent and the bridge that joins two shores are raised by men who labor on without faltering, to the praise of the God who gives skill to human hands.

events.fact: In the War of 1812, the frigate USS United States under Commodore Stephen Decatur defeated and captured the British frigate HMS Macedonian, bringing the prize home to a jubilant nation.

At the Battle off Samar in the Philippines, the tiny American escort force 'Taffy 3' charged a vastly superior Japanese fleet, sacrificing ships and men but turning the enemy back and saving the Leyte landings.

block: On October 25, 1812, Commodore Stephen Decatur drove the frigate USS United States into close action and battered the British HMS Macedonian into surrender, sailing his prize home to a nation hungry for proof that its sailors could best the masters of the sea. On the same day in 1944, the outgunned American destroyers and escort carriers of Taffy 3 hurled themselves at a Japanese battle fleet many times their strength off Samar, and at fearful cost in ships and lives they turned the enemy away and shielded the landings at Leyte. A Steadfast citizen fights with the resolve of Decatur and the desperate courage of those sailors, standing his ground against long odds and trusting God to give valor its due.

events.fact: The Erie Canal opened, completed after years of doubt and labor; Governor DeWitt Clinton sailed from Buffalo to New York Harbor and poured Lake Erie water into the sea in the 'Wedding of the Waters.'
The Pony Express ceased operations, its faithful riders giving way to the just-completed transcontinental telegraph after eighteen months of carrying the mail across the western wilderness.

block: On October 26, 1825, the Erie Canal opened at last, and Governor DeWitt Clinton sailed the length of what mockers had called 'Clinton's Ditch' to pour Lake Erie water into New York Harbor, vindicating years of derided toil that bound the frontier to the seaboard. On the same day in 1861, the Pony Express closed its run, its hard-riding couriers bowing out gracefully now that the telegraph had reached across the plains, their eighteen months of faithful service already the stuff of legend. A Steadfast citizen finishes what scoffers said could not be done as the canal builders did, and serves his post with honor to the end as those riders did, content that God measures the man by his faithfulness and not by the applause of the crowd.

events.fact: The first of the Federalist Papers appeared in a New York newspaper under the pen name 'Publius,' beginning the series by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay urging ratification of the Constitution.
Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th President of the United States, was born in New York City; a sickly boy, he built himself into a soldier, statesman, and tireless champion of the strenuous life.

block: On October 27, 1787, the first Federalist essay appeared over the signature of Publius, opening the patient, reasoned campaign by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay to persuade a wary people to adopt the Constitution by argument rather than force. On the same day in 1858, Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York City, a frail and asthmatic child who through dogged discipline forged himself into a robust soldier, hunter, and president. A Steadfast citizen wins his battles by perseverance as Publius won the argument for the Constitution, and overcomes his own weakness through steady effort as Roosevelt overcame his, asking God for the resolve to labor on and grow strong.

events.fact: The Massachusetts General Court voted to found a college at New Towne (Cambridge), the institution soon named Harvard, established chiefly to train a learned and godly ministry for the churches.
President Grover Cleveland dedicated the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor, the gift of the people of France, before a great crowd and a harbor full of ships.

block: On October 28, 1636, the Massachusetts General Court set aside four hundred pounds to found a college at Cambridge, soon called Harvard, that the churches might never be left to an unlearned ministry once the present pastors lay in the dust. On the same day in 1886, President Grover Cleveland dedicated the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor, the gift of France lifting her lamp above the gateway of a free nation. A Steadfast citizen treasures both the lamp of learning and the torch of liberty, guarding the godly schooling of his children as the Puritans did and the freedom won for him as a sacred trust, holding fast to what is good before the God who is the giver of every light.

events.fact: On 'Black Tuesday,' the stock market collapsed as some 16 million shares were dumped on the New York Stock Exchange, wiping out fortunes and ushering in the Great Depression.

The first message was sent over the ARPANET between computers at UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute; the system crashed after two letters, but an hour later the connection succeeded, marking the dawn of the internet.

block: On October 29, 1929, panic seized the New York Stock Exchange on Black Tuesday as sixteen million shares were thrown overboard and paper fortunes vanished in a day, a hard lesson that riches make themselves wings and fly away. On the same day in 1969, researchers at UCLA tried to send the first message over the ARPANET to Stanford, and though the machine crashed after only two letters, they steadied it and an hour later completed the link that would one day become the internet. A Steadfast citizen anchors his hope in God rather than in markets that crash, and like those persistent engineers he rises again after the first failure, building quietly toward what endures.

events.fact: John Adams, second President of the United States, signer of the Declaration of Independence, and tireless advocate of American independence, was born in Braintree, Massachusetts.

Orson Welles broadcast his radio dramatization of 'The War of the Worlds' over CBS, and some listeners who tuned in late mistook the realistic account of a Martian invasion for genuine news, sparking alarm.

block: On October 30, 1735, John Adams was born in Braintree, Massachusetts, the farmer's son who would argue America's case for independence with unbending conviction and serve her as her second president. On the same day in 1938, Orson Welles' realistic radio play of 'The War of the Worlds' convinced a portion of its hurried listeners that Martians had truly landed, a curious night that revealed how easily an anxious crowd may be swept along by rumor. A Steadfast citizen holds firm to principle as Adams did and keeps a sober, discerning mind when others are carried off by alarm, standing on what is true and trusting God rather than being tossed about by every panic and false report.

events.fact: Nevada was admitted to the Union as the 36th state in the midst of the Civil War, earning the motto 'Battle Born'; its constitution was sent by telegraph to Washington to ensure its vote for the Union.

After fourteen years of labor, sculptor Gutzon Borglum's colossal Mount Rushmore carving of Presidents Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, and Theodore Roosevelt was declared complete in the Black Hills of South Dakota.

block: On October 31, 1864, Nevada entered the Union as the 36th state amid the storm of the Civil War, so eager to stand with the nation that its whole constitution was wired to Washington, winning it the proud motto 'Battle Born.' On the same day in 1941, after fourteen years of dynamite, drill, and chisel, Gutzon Borglum's granite faces of Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, and Roosevelt were declared finished on Mount Rushmore, a monument hewn to outlast the ages. A Steadfast citizen commits himself for the long haul as Nevada committed itself to the Union and as those carvers gave fourteen years to the rock, laboring at enduring work and entrusting its fruit to the God who is Himself the Rock that never fails.
